Efficient Large-Integer Arithmetic for FHE

IACR ePrint 2026/1608 (preprint) · full view ↗

Overview and scope

This is a survey, not a new construction. Eight authors from Duality Technologies, Fair Math, and NVIDIA trace how large-integer arithmetic in RLWE-based FHE libraries evolved from arbitrary-precision (multiprecision) integers to the Residue Number System (RNS) backends that underpin practically every modern implementation, and then to the recent refinements that recover, from inside the residue world, the flexibility that multiprecision arithmetic gave away.

The central claim organizing the article: in a residue representation, almost everything is easy. Additions, subtractions, multiplications, and the NTT all run channel-by-channel in single precision. The only operations that genuinely resist a residue-wise implementation are those that depend on the magnitude of the represented value as an integer, and all of them reduce to two primitives, RNS basis extension and RNS scaling. Two algorithmic families realize those primitives: the integer-only approach of Bajard, Eynard, Hasan, and Zucca (BEHZ), and the floating-point approach of Halevi, Polyakov, and Shoup (HPS). Everything else in a modern library, including modulus switching, CKKS rescaling, hybrid key switching, BFV multiplication, and bootstrapping, is a composition of those two primitives around cheap component-wise work.

The presentation is deliberately scheme-generic: the primitives apply equally to BFV, BGV, and CKKS, with CKKS used as the running concrete example because of its dominance in privacy-preserving machine learning.

From the ePrint listing metadata rather than the paper body: category Implementation, status preprint (received 2026-08-04, approved 2026-08-06), licensed CC BY.

The problem: ring arithmetic versus machine words

All schemes considered operate over the power-of-two cyclotomic ring

$$R_Q = \mathbb{Z}_Q[X]/(X^N + 1),$$

with $N$ a power of two and $Q$ the coefficient modulus. Ciphertexts are tuples of polynomials with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}_Q$, and every homomorphic operation (addition, multiplication, modulus switching / rescaling, key switching, bootstrapping) reduces to arithmetic on those coefficients. Cost is therefore dominated by modular additions, multiplications, and reductions modulo $Q$.

Notation. $\mathbb{Z}_n$ is identified with the symmetric interval $\mathbb{Z} \cap [-n/2, n/2)$; $[x]_n$ denotes centered reduction into that interval, and $|x|_n \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ the non-negative representative when the distinction matters. $\lfloor x \rfloor$, $\lceil x \rceil$, and $\lceil x \rfloor$ denote rounding down, up, and to nearest, extended element-wise to vectors and polynomial coefficients. Modern implementations pick $Q = \prod_i q_i$ as a product of pairwise coprime machine-word-sized primes; a generic modulus of this form is written $q = \prod_{i=1}^{k} q_i$.

Practical parameters. Maximal $\log_2 Q$ at the 128-bit security level for uniform ternary secrets and Gaussian error with $\sigma = 3.19$, reproduced from Table 5.2 of the homomorphic encryption security guidelines, together with the functionality typically instantiated at each ring dimension:

Ring dimension $N$Max. $\log_2 Q$Typical functionalityRepresentative applications

The consequence is stark. At $N = 2^{14}$ a ciphertext is two or more polynomials of 16,384 coefficients each, modulo an integer of several hundred bits, so a single homomorphic multiplication requires millions of modular operations on integers far wider than the 64-bit words commodity processors support natively. These bounds match the default parameter validation performed by libraries such as OpenFHE. This mismatch is the driving force behind the whole evolution the article traces.

First generation: arbitrary-precision arithmetic

Early libraries represented coefficients modulo $Q$ with multiprecision integers, closely following the mathematical formulation and reusing mature arithmetic backends. HElib used NTL, which in turn used GMP. Even at that stage HElib was already hybrid: its DoubleCRT representation applied RNS techniques to selected operations while depending on multiprecision arithmetic elsewhere. The initial versions of Microsoft SEAL and PALISADE likewise targeted BFV with multiprecision arithmetic. DARPA's PROCEED program is credited with motivating much of the research into faster multiprecision and RNS techniques.

What it bought: a natural correspondence with the mathematics, straightforward implementation, easy correctness verification, and reuse of well-tested libraries. What it cost: low performance, frequent cache misses, expensive modular multiplication and reduction, and dynamic memory management overhead. Arbitrary-precision arithmetic quickly became the primary bottleneck for practical workloads.

From partial to Full RNS: the library evolution

Early libraries already used the polynomial CRT decomposition via the NTT. Applying the CRT to the coefficient modulus itself, that is the integer CRT or RNS, replaces multiprecision operations with collections of independent small-integer modular operations. HElib was first, through DoubleCRT: a polynomial is stored separately modulo each small prime $q_i$, each residue in NTT form. The name reflects the two independent CRT decompositions, one over the polynomial ring and one over the coefficient modulus.

What the partial-RNS stage did not fix

  • Constrained moduli. Each $q_i$ had to be NTT-friendly, that is $q_i \equiv 1 \pmod{2N}$, so parameter selection became far more restrictive than in the arbitrary-precision setting.
  • Representation churn. Libraries repeatedly performed inverse NTTs to recover coefficient representation for certain algorithms and forward NTTs to return to the transform domain. A substantial fraction of runtime went to conversions rather than arithmetic.
  • Magnitude-dependent steps still positional. Divide-and-round and base-decomposition inside decryption, multiplication, modulus switching, and key switching all reverted to multiprecision arithmetic.

Full RNS

BEHZ gave the first Full RNS variant of BFV, replacing the remaining multiprecision operations with residue-wise basis extension and scaling. SEAL adopted it and became the first major library with a Full RNS BFV (versions $\geq$ 2.3.0). HPS refined the direction, simplifying and cheapening both primitives, and was implemented in PALISADE (v1.1+). An implementation study compared both variants on CPUs and GPUs, initially observing better noise scaling for HPS with increasing depth, a gap later traced by Bajard et al. to an implementation deviation in the BEHZ correction procedure rather than to the variant itself.

For approximate encryption the transition was slower. HEAAN's first CKKS implementation used arbitrary-precision arithmetic, with DoubleCRT mainly for polynomial multiplication. Because CKKS rescales after every multiplication, extending Full RNS to approximate arithmetic required new techniques for rescaling and modulus switching directly on residues while preserving accuracy. Cheon, Han, Kim, Kim, and Song supplied them with a Full RNS CKKS featuring an RNS-friendly modulus structure and an approximate rescaling procedure on residues. Around the same time, groups independently built Full RNS CKKS in SEAL, PALISADE, and HElib, several evaluated in the iDASH 2018 competition.

Full RNS is now the default backend architecture (SEAL, OpenFHE, Lattigo). The achievement is that ciphertexts stay in RNS form across nearly all operations, avoiding reconstruction into large integers and enabling native word arithmetic and SIMD. The costs, however, are real: the NTT-friendliness constraint is inherited, basis extension and key switching need substantial precomputation and careful memory management, and for CKKS the rescaling granularity is set by the bit sizes of the available primes, making precision management rigid and introducing an inherent scaling error. Full RNS solved the primary performance bottleneck and shifted the complexity to modulus-chain construction, basis management, precision control, and memory-efficient data movement. As the authors put it, modern libraries are not merely "using RNS"; their performance depends critically on how the entire RNS backend is engineered.

The RNS toolkit and why magnitude is the obstacle

Fix an RNS base $\mathcal{B} = \{q_1, \dots, q_k\}$ of pairwise coprime single-precision moduli, so $\gcd(q_i, q_j) = 1$ for $i \neq j$, and let $q = \prod_{i=1}^{k} q_i$. By the CRT the map $x \mapsto (x_1, \dots, x_k)$ with $x_i = [x]_{q_i}$ is a ring isomorphism $\mathbb{Z}_q \cong \mathbb{Z}_{q_1} \times \cdots \times \mathbb{Z}_{q_k}$; write $x \sim (x_1, \dots, x_k)$. Additions, subtractions, and multiplications proceed component-wise, independently and in parallel, entirely in single precision. The quantity $q$ is the dynamic range: the representation is unique as long as $x \in \mathbb{Z} \cap [-q/2, q/2)$.

The inverse map is CRT reconstruction:

$$x = \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{k} x_i \cdot \left[ \left(\tfrac{q}{q_i}\right)^{-1} \right]_{q_i} \cdot \frac{q}{q_i} \right]_q .$$

Two ways of making the outer reduction modulo $q$ explicit are used pervasively:

$$x = \left( \sum_{i=1}^{k} \left[ x_i \cdot \left[ \left(\tfrac{q}{q_i}\right)^{-1} \right]_{q_i} \right]_{q_i} \cdot \frac{q}{q_i} \right) - \upsilon \cdot q, \qquad \upsilon \in \mathbb{Z},\ |\upsilon| \leq k/2,$$ $$x = \left( \sum_{i=1}^{k} x_i \cdot \left[ \left(\tfrac{q}{q_i}\right)^{-1} \right]_{q_i} \cdot \frac{q}{q_i} \right) - \upsilon' \cdot q, \qquad \upsilon' \in \mathbb{Z},\ |\upsilon'| \leq \tfrac{k}{2}\max_i (q_i).$$

The correction terms $\upsilon$ and $\upsilon'$ absorb the missing final reduction modulo $q$. These identities are the source of both the power and the difficulty of RNS: the sums are computable residue-wise, but $\upsilon$ and $\upsilon'$ encode global magnitude information that no single residue channel can see.

The three magnitude-dependent patterns

  1. Lifting. Interpret $x \in \mathbb{Z}_q$ as an integer in $[-q/2, q/2)$ and re-represent it modulo a larger $Q = q \cdot p$, for instance before a BFV tensor product whose result must not wrap around, or when raising a ciphertext digit to an extended basis during key switching.
  2. Scaling and rounding. Compute $y = \left\lceil \tfrac{t}{q} x \right\rfloor$ for $t \ll q$: BFV decryption and multiplication, CKKS rescaling, modulus switching in all schemes, and the final scale-down of key switching.
  3. Digit decomposition. Split $x$ into low-norm digits whose recombination is linear, used by all key-switching methods to control noise growth.

All three depend on the magnitude of $x$ as an integer, not merely on its residues, and so appear to require conversion back to a positional representation, negating the benefit of RNS. The literature's answer: primitives that perform (i) and (ii) directly on residues, plus the observation that (iii) can be sidestepped entirely by redefining the decomposition to be the RNS decomposition, whose digits are free.

Fast basis extension: BEHZ versus HPS

Let $x \in \mathbb{Z}_q$ be given in CRT form with respect to $\mathcal{B} = \{q_1, \dots, q_k\}$ and let $\mathcal{B}' = \{p_1, \dots, p_{k'}\}$ be a second base coprime to the first, with $p = \prod_j p_j$. Basis extension computes the residues of $x$, or of a value congruent to $x$ modulo $q$, with respect to $\mathcal{B}'$, yielding a representation in $\mathcal{B} \cup \mathcal{B}'$ with dynamic range $qp$. Both families share the channel-local first step $y_i := \left[ x_i \cdot \left[ (q/q_i)^{-1} \right]_{q_i} \right]_{q_i}$, computed in single precision and in parallel over $i$. They differ only in how the quotient $\upsilon$ is handled.

BEHZ: approximate conversion with integer-only correction

The BEHZ fast base conversion applies the third displayed identity without computing $\upsilon$:

$$\mathsf{FastBaseConv}(x, \mathcal{B}, \mathcal{B}') = \left( \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{k} \left[ x_i \cdot \left[ \left(\tfrac{q}{q_i}\right)^{-1} \right]_{q_i} \right]_{q_i} \cdot \frac{q}{q_i} \right]_{p_j} \right)_{p_j \in \mathcal{B}'} .$$

With the constants $[q/q_i]_{p_j}$ precomputed, this needs only single-precision operations. It is CRT reconstruction without the final reduction modulo the dynamic range: the converted value equals $x + \upsilon q$ for a small $q$-overflow $\upsilon$, so the result represents $x$ only up to a small multiple of $q$.

Sometimes the overflow merely inflates noise and can be tolerated. When it must be removed, BEHZ augments the base with two redundant moduli:

  • Small Montgomery reduction (input side). Inputs are pre-multiplied by $\tilde{m}$; after conversion the residue channel modulo $\tilde{m}$ reveals $\upsilon$, which is subtracted, and the factor $\tilde{m}$ is divided out. The correction leaves a small additive term that must be tracked in the noise analysis. Stated as Algorithm 1 in the appendix below.
  • Shenoy-Kumaresan extension (output side). A modulus $m_{sk}$ carried through the entire computation is used at the end to recover $\upsilon$ exactly, producing an exact conversion back to the original base. Classical, used as a black box.

The article states the small Montgomery reduction in full because its exact specification turns out to be load-bearing: a slight deviation from it is the crux of the noise-growth episode discussed further below. Note that $m_{sk}$ appears in Algorithm 1 only as a carried residue channel and plays no role in the reduction itself. The net effect is a fully integer pipeline, at the cost of (a) additional residue channels $\tilde{m}$, $m_{sk}$, and a further modulus $\gamma$ for decryption, (b) extra modular multiplications for the corrections, and (c) additional noise-analysis terms.

HPS: exact conversion via floating-point estimation

HPS computes the correction quotient directly. Observing that

$$\upsilon = \left\lceil \sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{1}{q_i} \left[ x_i \cdot \left[ \left(\tfrac{q}{q_i}\right)^{-1} \right]_{q_i} \right]_{q_i} \right\rfloor ,$$

one computes $y_i$ in single-precision integer arithmetic, forms the ratios $z_i := y_i / q_i \in [-\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2})$ in floating point, sums them, and rounds. With $\upsilon$ in hand the exact extension follows:

$$\mathsf{FastBaseExt}(x, \mathcal{B}, \mathcal{B}') = \left( \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{k} y_i \cdot \left[ \frac{q}{q_i} \right]_{p_j} - \upsilon \cdot [q]_{p_j} \right]_{p_j} \right)_{p_j \in \mathcal{B}'} ,$$

with $[q/q_i]_{p_j}$ and $[q]_{p_j}$ precomputed. No auxiliary moduli and no correction pass.

Correctness and precision of the estimate

The sole error source is the floating-point estimate of $\upsilon$. Instead of the exact $z_i$ one computes approximations with per-term error $\epsilon_i$, so the computed $\upsilon^{*} = \left\lceil \sum_i (z_i + \epsilon_i) \right\rfloor$ can differ from $\upsilon$ when the exact sum lands in the narrow error region $\mathbb{Z} + \tfrac{1}{2} \pm \epsilon$ with $\epsilon = \sum_i \epsilon_i$. With IEEE 754 doubles, $|\epsilon_i| < 2^{-53}$, hence $|\epsilon| < k \, 2^{-53}$, for example $|\epsilon| < 2^{-48}$ for $k \leq 32$. Three regimes make this benign:

  • When $|x| \ll q$, for instance $|x| < q/4$ as guaranteed in the second extension inside key switching and in the scale-down after tensoring where $p$ is chosen substantially larger than $q$, the exact sum is bounded away from $\mathbb{Z} + \tfrac{1}{2}$ and the estimate is provably always correct.
  • When $x$ is (pseudo)random in $\mathbb{Z}_q$, the probability of landing in the error region is bounded by $2|\epsilon|$, negligible in practice.
  • Even when an off-by-one does occur, it merely contributes $q$ to a value that is subsequently interpreted modulo $q$ or scaled down, adding at most 1 to 2 bits of ciphertext noise in the worst case and unobservable in experiments.

Crucially, the estimate imposes no constraint on the sizes of the moduli themselves: every summand $z_i = y_i / q_i$ lies in $[-\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2})$, so the floating-point error is relative to a bounded quantity and independent of $\max_i (q_i)$. Full word-sized moduli are supported with plain doubles. A moduli-size constraint does arise from floating-point precision, but in the scaling procedures, where fractional constants multiply full-sized residues.

Scaling in RNS: simple and complex

The second magnitude-dependent primitive is scaling with rounding: given $x \in \mathbb{Z}_q$ in CRT form and an integer $t \geq 2$ with $t \ll q$, compute

$$y = \left[ \left\lceil \frac{t}{q} \cdot x \right\rfloor \right]_t .$$

This is the core of BFV decryption, and the same pattern of dividing by a subproduct of the modulus and rounding appears in modulus switching and CKKS rescaling.

HPS simple scaling

Starting from the fourth displayed identity and multiplying by $t/q$, the term $\upsilon' t$ vanishes modulo $t$, giving

$$y = \left[ \left\lceil \sum_{i=1}^{k} x_i \cdot \left[ \left(\tfrac{q}{q_i}\right)^{-1} \right]_{q_i} \cdot \frac{t}{q_i} \right\rfloor \right]_t .$$

The rational constants are precomputed and split into integral and fractional parts, $\left[ t \cdot \left[ (q/q_i)^{-1} \right]_{q_i} \right] / q_i = \omega_i + \theta_i$ with $\omega_i \in \mathbb{Z}_t$ and $\theta_i \in [-\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2})$, storing $\omega_i$ as single-precision integers and $\theta_i$ as (extended) doubles. At runtime one computes $w := \left[ \sum_i x_i \omega_i \right]_t$ in integer arithmetic and $v := \left\lceil \sum_i x_i \theta_i \right\rfloor$ in floating point, and outputs $[w + v]_t$.

In decryption the ciphertext noise guarantees the pre-rounding value is within $1/4$ of an integer, so restricting $q_i \leq 2^{\nu - 1} / k$, with $\nu$ the significand precision in bits, ensures exactness. This tightens the textbook correctness bound by at most one bit, from $(\Delta - r_t(q))/2$ to $(\Delta - r_t(q))/4$, where $\Delta = \lfloor q/t \rfloor$ and $r_t(q) = q - t\Delta$.

Here the floating-point precision does constrain moduli size, unlike in basis extension: the fractional constants $\theta_i$, stored with absolute error $\sim 2^{-\nu}$, multiply full-sized residues $x_i$, so the error budget scales with $\max_i (q_i)$. For decryption-type scaling with double precision ($\nu = 53$) the requirement $q_i \leq 2^{\nu-1}/k$ limits the usable moduli for signed-integer modular arithmetic; extended double precision ($\nu = 65$, the x86 long double) supports moduli up to 59 bits, and software double-double ($\nu = 113$) supports the full 60-bit range at significant performance cost. In the original HPS formulation this trade-off among $\nu$, $\max_i (q_i)$, and $k$ was a distinctive engineering constraint: HPS was fastest exactly when native floating-point types sufficed. Kim, Polyakov, and Zucca removed it by decomposing the input residues into smaller digits before the floating-point summation, so the full range of word-sized CRT moduli (up to 60 bits) is supported with regular double precision alone, with no extended or emulated precision.

BEHZ simple scaling

BEHZ replaces rounding by exact flooring, which is compatible with integer-only RNS:

$$\left\lfloor \frac{t}{q} [x]_q \right\rfloor = \frac{t \, [x]_q - |t x|_q}{q},$$

an exact integer division. Modulo $t$ the first term cancels, and $-|t x|_q / q$ is obtained via $\mathsf{FastBaseConv}$ from base $q$ to $t$. Because the fast conversion is inexact, a redundant modulus $\gamma$ is introduced: the computation runs simultaneously modulo $t$ and modulo $\gamma$, and the $\gamma$-channel both cancels the $q$-overflow and corrects the flooring-versus-rounding discrepancy. The auxiliary channel slightly reduces the tolerable noise: correctness requires $\lVert e \rVert_{\infty} \leq \Delta \left( \tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{k}{\gamma} \right) - \tfrac{|q|_t}{2}$, approaching the textbook bound only as $\gamma \gg k$.

Complex scaling: scaling out of an extended base

The most demanding pattern combines both primitives. After a tensor-style multiplication the intermediate value lives in an extended base, $x \in \mathbb{Z} \cap [-qp/2t, qp/2t)$ represented in $\mathcal{B} \cup \mathcal{B}' = \{q_1, \dots, q_k, p_1, \dots, p_{k'}\}$, and one must compute $y = \left[ \left\lceil \tfrac{t}{q} \cdot x \right\rfloor \right]_q$, that is scale by $t/q$ and land back in the original base. Writing $Q := qp$, so that $Q/q_i = (q/q_i)p$ and $Q/p_j = q(p/p_j)$, the HPS formulation takes two steps:

  1. Scale within the complementary base. Apply simple scaling with $q' = qp$ and $t' = tp$, producing $y' := \left[ \lceil t/q \cdot x \rfloor \right]_p$ directly in $\mathcal{B}'$. Because $|x| < qp/2t$ the scaled value lies in $[-p/2, p/2)$, so the mod-$p$ representation determines $y'$ exactly, without modular reduction. Concretely, with precomputed splits $\left[ t \cdot \left[ (Q/q_i)^{-1} \right]_{q_i} \cdot p \right] / q_i = \omega'_i + \theta'_i$, $\omega'_i \in \mathbb{Z}_p$, $\theta'_i \in [-\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2})$, and constants $\lambda_j := \left[ t \cdot \left[ (Q/p_j)^{-1} \right]_{p_j} \cdot (p/p_j) \right]_{p_j}$, one computes $v := \left\lceil \sum_i \theta'_i x_i \right\rfloor$ once and $y'_j := \left[ \lambda_j x'_j + \sum_i [\omega'_i]_{p_j} x_i + v \right]_{p_j}$ for each $j$.
  2. Extend back. Apply $\mathsf{FastBaseExt}$ to extend $y'$ from $\mathcal{B}'$ to $\mathcal{B}$, then discard the $\mathcal{B}'$ components. Because $|y'| \leq q/2 \ll p/2$, this second extension provably never lands in the floating-point error region: exactness comes for free from the parameter choice $p > q$.

Rounding here need not be exact; a rounding error simply adds to the ciphertext noise, in contrast to decryption where exactness is required. The BEHZ counterpart follows the same blueprint with integer-only tools: lifting via $\mathsf{FastBaseConv}$ with input-side pre-multiplication by $\tilde{m}$ and small Montgomery reduction to remove $q$-overflows, approximate flooring in the complementary base, and an exact return via Shenoy-Kumaresan using the carried modulus $m_{sk}$. The auxiliary channels $\{\tilde{m}, m_{sk}\}$ ride along through the tensor product, adding NTTs and modular multiplications throughout.

BEHZ versus HPS: the verdict, and a cautionary episode

The contrast reduces to three axes.

  • Arithmetic model. BEHZ is integer-only, so its correctness is unconditional and its behavior independent of the floating-point environment. HPS estimates the reconstruction quotient in floating point, trading a small, controllable approximation-error probability for the elimination of all auxiliary moduli and correction passes, and in its original formulation tying the supported moduli sizes in the scaling procedures to the available floating-point precision (a limitation later lifted).
  • Auxiliary machinery. BEHZ needs $\tilde{m}$, $m_{sk}$, and $\gamma$ for decryption, which add residue channels, precomputed tables, and parameter-selection constraints. HPS needs none, which makes it simpler to implement and its parameter generation independent of the arithmetic backend.
  • Noise behavior. The HPS procedures add at most about 2 bits of noise relative to the textbook scheme at any depth, and the worst-case analyses of the two variants are essentially equivalent.

The noise-growth episode

This is the article's most instructive implementation lesson. The initial experimental comparison observed markedly faster practical noise growth for BEHZ, with HPS reaching a multiplicative depth typically 15 to 30 percent larger at the same parameters, and attributed it to correlations introduced by the fast-conversion overflow term $\upsilon q$, which would invalidate the average-case (Central Limit Theorem) noise heuristics. A subsequent note by Bajard et al. identified the actual cause: the implementations of the small Montgomery reduction $\mathsf{SmMRq}_{\tilde{m}}$ in SEAL and PALISADE deviated slightly from the original BEHZ specification. Once fixed, both variants reach the same multiplicative depth in practice, and the average-case noise behavior of a correctly implemented BEHZ matches that of HPS.

The takeaway cuts both ways: the correction machinery of the integer-only approach is subtle enough that a small implementation deviation, invisible to worst-case analysis, silently cost dozens of levels of multiplicative depth. That removes the noise-growth argument against BEHZ while reinforcing the implementation-simplicity argument for HPS.

Kim, Polyakov, and Zucca further improved the HPS procedures beyond removing the floating-point precision constraint: they reduced the noise growth of the multiplication pipeline and extended the same RNS toolkit to an improved BGV instantiation, unifying the treatment of the exact schemes. These trade-offs explain the adoption pattern: SEAL's first Full RNS BFV used BEHZ, PALISADE adopted HPS (with BEHZ added for the experimental comparison), and OpenFHE implements the improved HPS-style variants as its default.

Modulus switching, CKKS rescaling, and the three fixes

Throughout this part the modulus is a chain $Q_{\ell} = \prod_{i=0}^{\ell} q_i$ of NTT-friendly primes and ciphertexts at level $\ell$ live in $R_{Q_{\ell}}^2$. Modulus switching maps a ciphertext modulo $Q_{\ell}$ to one modulo $Q_{\ell-1} = Q_{\ell}/q_{\ell}$ encrypting approximately the same plaintext, by computing $c' = \left\lceil \tfrac{Q_{\ell-1}}{Q_{\ell}} c \right\rfloor = \lceil c/q_{\ell} \rfloor$, a special case of simple scaling. In BGV it controls noise; in BFV it compresses a result before sending it to the decryptor or reduces the cost of later operations; in CKKS the identical operation, called rescaling, additionally reduces the encrypted scale, implementing fixed-point precision management.

One observation makes it lightweight in RNS: since $q_{\ell}$ is itself one of the RNS moduli, no generic scaling procedure is needed. Writing the division with explicit rounding error,

$$c' = \frac{c - [c]_{q_{\ell}}}{q_{\ell}}, \qquad \text{i.e.} \qquad c'_i = \left[ q_{\ell}^{-1} \left( c_i - [c]_{q_{\ell}} \right) \right]_{q_i} \ \text{for } i < \ell ,$$

one needs only the residue $[c]_{q_{\ell}}$ (one inverse NTT in the dropped channel if the ciphertext is kept in evaluation representation), its broadcast into the remaining channels, and one modular multiplication by the precomputed $[q_{\ell}^{-1}]_{q_i}$ per channel. This is the RNS-friendly rescaling introduced for CKKS by Cheon, Han, Kim, Kim, and Song, and the analogous BGV modulus switching, with an extra correction added to preserve the plaintext value, used since HElib.

The structural cost

Rescaling granularity is now tied to the modulus chain. One can only divide by primes, or products of primes, actually present in the chain; rescaling by an arbitrary small amount, say 10 bits, is impossible unless the chain was explicitly designed with such primes. This couples numerical-precision management to modulus-chain design and makes parameter selection more rigid. It also introduces a persistent scaling error: NTT primes can only approximate the target scaling factor ($q_{\ell} \approx 2^{\Delta}$ but never exactly), so every rescaling in the original Full RNS variant perturbs the encrypted scale and the accumulated deviation shows up as additional approximation error in decrypted results. This error is inherent to the RNS formulation and absent from multiprecision CKKS, where the scaling factor can be an exact power of two. Three lines of work address it.

1. Eliminating the scaling error: reduced-error CKKS

Kim, Papadimitriou, and Polyakov showed the scaling error can be eliminated outright without changing the modulus chain. Instead of pretending every level shares a common scaling factor $\Delta$, their variant maintains an exact, level-dependent scaling factor tracking the primes actually consumed: after a multiplication at scale $\Delta_{\ell}$ is rescaled by $q_{\ell}$, the scale becomes $\Delta_{\ell-1} = \Delta_{\ell}^2 / q_{\ell}$. Subsequent operations are adjusted, with scalar corrections inserted automatically when operands at different scales meet, so all arithmetic remains exact with respect to the tracked scale. Combined with a reduced-error encryption procedure that pushes fresh LWE noise below the significant bits of the message, this recovers several bits of precision, roughly 4 bits for uniform ternary secrets and up to 12 bits relative to prior RNS implementations depending on the setting, at essentially no performance cost. Implemented in OpenFHE as the FLEXIBLEAUTO and FLEXIBLEAUTOEXT rescaling modes, which are the library defaults. In HElib and Lattigo, similar exact-scale tracking is not a selectable mode but the built-in behavior of the evaluator.

2. Scaling factors beyond the word size: composite scaling

Precision above remains capped by the machine word: a single-prime scaling factor cannot exceed the word size $W$, which is limiting on 32-bit hardware accelerators (GPUs, ASICs) and for high-precision applications. Composite scaling lifts the cap by composing each scaling factor from $d \geq 2$ smaller NTT primes with $\prod_{j=1}^{d} q_{\ell,j} \approx 2^{\Delta}$; rescaling drops $d$ primes from the chain at once, exactly as in the modulus-switching equation applied iteratively. This makes scaling factors of 64 bits or more available on architectures with a smaller native word, and it composes with reduced-error exact scale tracking. The authors prove and experimentally confirm functional equivalence with single-prime scaling. Integrated in OpenFHE as composite scaling modes and also implemented in Lattigo.

3. Decoupling scale from modulus: grafting

Grafting attacks the root cause, the rigid coupling between scale factors (a numerical-precision concern) and the RNS factors of the modulus (a cryptographic one). The ciphertext modulus is assembled from reusable, word-size-optimized factors called sprouts, including power-of-two factors that need not be NTT primes. Rescaling by an arbitrary number of bits is then realized as a modulus-switching step rather than by dropping designated chain primes, since consecutive moduli are no longer divisible by one another. This removes both the scaling error and the NTT-prime scarcity problem (large chains of small primes for a given ring dimension), and it improves performance by packing the modulus into full machine-word limbs, giving fewer, denser RNS channels for the same modulus size. Adopted in HEAAN-family implementations and in recent GPU libraries.

Taken together, the three refinements illustrate a recurring pattern of the Full RNS era: the residue representation first trades exactness or flexibility for speed, and subsequent work recovers the lost property (exact scales, large scaling factors, arbitrary rescaling) by more careful bookkeeping on top of the same residue-level primitives.

Key switching and its hybrid RNS form

Key switching converts a ciphertext component decryptable under a key $s'$ (for example $s^2$ after multiplication, or a rotated key after an automorphism) into one decryptable under $s$. All modern constructions share the same skeleton: decompose the input $c$ into low-norm digits $\{c^{(j)}\}$ whose recombination is linear, take an inner product with key-switching keys that encrypt the correspondingly weighted multiples of $s'$, and, in modern variants, scale the result back down. The decomposition exists solely to control the noise term $\sum_j \langle e_j, c^{(j)} \rangle$: smaller digits mean less noise but more NTTs and larger keys.

Milestones

  1. Positional digit decomposition (BV). Decompose each coefficient in a radix $w$: $c = \sum_j c^{(j)} w^j$. In RNS form this is exactly pattern (iii): extracting base-$w$ digits of a multi-hundred-bit integer is a positional operation requiring full CRT reconstruction, precisely what RNS is meant to avoid.
  2. Auxiliary-modulus raising (GHS). Avoid decomposition entirely by lifting $c$ from $R_Q$ to $R_{QP}$ for a special modulus $P > Q$, multiplying by a key-switching key defined modulo $QP$, and scaling back down by $P$. The key noise is divided by $P$ and becomes negligible, but requiring $P > Q$ doubles the effective modulus, which at fixed security halves the usable ciphertext modulus budget. A hybrid BV-GHS method was also proposed in the same work.
  3. BV RNS digit decomposition. Bajard et al. observed, with a refinement in HPS, that the CRT decomposition itself can serve as the digit decomposition. The map $c \mapsto \left( [c]_{q_1}, \dots, [c]_{q_k} \right)$ is linear via recombination with weights $\left[ (q/q_i)^{-1} \right]_{q_i} \cdot (q/q_i)$, its digits $[c]_{q_i}$ are available for free in an RNS representation, and their norms are bounded by $q_i/2 \approx w/2$. The evaluation key is generated with respect to the weights $\left[ \left[ (q/q_i)^{-1} \right]_{q_i} \cdot (q/q_i) \cdot s' \right]_Q$, equivalently keys that are $[s']_{q_i}$ in channel $i$ and $0$ elsewhere. This eliminates both the decomposition cost and, in the refined formulation, all precomputed decomposition constants.
  4. Hybrid key switching in RNS. The GHS hybrid method was extended to CKKS in its modern RNS form by Han and Ki and adapted to BGV/BFV by Kim, Polyakov, and Zucca. It combines (b) and (c) and is the default in OpenFHE, SEAL (for CKKS/BGV), Lattigo, and HEAAN.

Hybrid key switching, step by step

The RNS base of $Q_{\ell}$ is partitioned into $d$ groups ("digits") $\mathcal{D}_1, \dots, \mathcal{D}_d$ with partial products $\hat{Q}_j$, and a special modulus $P = \prod_j p_j$ is chosen with $P \gtrsim \max_j \hat{Q}_j$, that is only as large as one digit, not as large as all of $Q_{\ell}$. For input $c \in R_{Q_{\ell}}$:

  1. Decompose. Split the RNS representation into the $d$ digit groups $c^{(j)} = \left( [c]_{q_i} \right)_{q_i \in \mathcal{D}_j}$. The splitting is free, but NTTs are typically required to convert the input from evaluation to coefficient representation before extracting digits.
  2. ModUp (basis extension). Extend each digit from its base $\mathcal{D}_j$ to the full base $\mathcal{B}_{Q_{\ell}} \cup \mathcal{B}_P$ using fast basis extension: $d$ invocations of $\mathsf{FastBaseExt}$, or $\mathsf{FastBaseConv}$ with or without corrections. This is where the magnitude of each digit, an integer bounded by $\hat{Q}_j/2$, is re-encoded in the larger dynamic range $Q_{\ell} P$. The extended digits are then converted to evaluation representation with additional NTTs.
  3. Inner product. Multiply the raised digits by the key-switching keys $\mathsf{ksk}_j \in R_{Q_{\ell}P}^2$, which encrypt $\left[ P \cdot \left[ (Q_{\ell}/\hat{Q}_j)^{-1} \right]_{\hat{Q}_j} \cdot (Q_{\ell}/\hat{Q}_j) \cdot s' \right]_{Q_{\ell}P}$, and accumulate, entirely component-wise in evaluation representation.
  4. ModDown (complex scaling). Scale the accumulated result by $1/P$ with rounding and return to base $\mathcal{B}_{Q_{\ell}}$: $\mathsf{ModDown}(x) = \left[ \lceil x/P \rfloor \right]_{Q_{\ell}}$, an instance of complex scaling with the roles of the two bases exchanged. Since the result is needed only in $\mathcal{B}_{Q_{\ell}}$, here the complementary base, the first step already produces it and the concluding extension back is not required. The key noise is attenuated by the factor $P$. NTTs are typically required to return to evaluation representation.

The digit-count knob. $d = k$ (one prime per digit) recovers pure RNS decomposition with minimal $P$, hence the most modulus budget for depth, and maximal NTT count plus the largest key material; $d = 1$ recovers GHS with minimal computation and maximal $P$. In practice $d$ is a tuning knob balancing key size, noise budget, and the $O(d \cdot (k + k'))$ NTTs that dominate key-switching time. Viewed through the lens of the survey, hybrid key switching is nothing more than a careful composition of the two magnitude-dependent primitives, $d$ basis extensions up and one complex scaling down, wrapped around cheap residue-wise inner products.

BFV multiplication as a composition

For completeness the article notes how the same blocks assemble into BFV homomorphic multiplication, the setting in which BEHZ and HPS were originally formulated. Tensoring requires products without wraparound, so ciphertexts are first lifted from $\mathcal{B}_q$ to $\mathcal{B}_q \cup \mathcal{B}_p$ (basis extension, 4 conversions), the tensor products are computed in the extended base with $qp \gtrsim$ the largest tensored coefficient, the three resulting components are scaled by $t/q$ back into $\mathcal{B}_q$ (complex scaling, 3 invocations), and the quadratic component is relinearized via RNS-digit key switching. Decryption is a single simple-scaling invocation. The cost of the full pipeline is exactly the sum of these building-block costs, which is why the BEHZ/HPS comparison transfers to any scheme built from the same blocks.

GPU acceleration

In the Full RNS setting most operations decompose into independent work across polynomial coefficients, RNS limbs, and even multiple ciphertexts in batched workloads. This maps naturally onto GPUs: modular additions and multiplications are data-parallel, NTTs decompose into parallel butterfly stages, and the basis-extension and ModDown kernels of key switching consist of large amounts of regular, matrix-like arithmetic (the inner products across residue channels).

Reported results:

  • BFV, HPS variant on GPU: homomorphic multiplication in 51 ms at multiplicative depth 98 and 128-bit security, two orders of magnitude faster than the CPU results, with HPS consistently outperforming BEHZ by 1.1 to 1.3 times on GPUs, where its avoidance of auxiliary residue channels pays off directly in fewer kernels and smaller constant-memory footprints.
  • FIDESlib, a state-of-the-art GPU-accelerated Full RNS CKKS library, illustrates that GPUs alleviate the bandwidth bottleneck of CKKS relative to DDR-based CPUs. This matters because modern FHE workloads are often limited by memory bandwidth and data movement as much as by computation; GPUs provide large register files, high-throughput GDDR/HBM memory, and increasingly large on-chip caches, placing them in an important middle ground between CPUs and custom ASICs.
  • Phantom supports accelerated leveled CKKS as well as BGV and BFV.
  • Cheddar supports fully bootstrappable CKKS, achieving bootstrapping in about 22 ms and encrypted ResNet-20 inference in about 720 ms on an NVIDIA RTX 5090.
  • Multi-GPU: FIDESlib supports multi-GPU contexts, and Cerium evaluates a CKKS bootstrap in under 8 ms across 8 NVIDIA B200 GPUs, plus an encrypted Llama3-8B inference in 134 s.

Among vectorized schemes, CKKS has attracted the most GPU effort, both because of its popularity for machine learning and because its bootstrapping is relatively efficient compared with BFV and BGV, which require costly digit-decomposition subroutines. The state-of-the-art GPU results for private LLM inference are covered in a separate 2026 SoK by some of the same authors.

A renewed interest in positional arithmetic

After a decisive migration away from positional representations, a recent line of work revisits them, arguing that some structural costs of Full RNS are avoidable if big-number arithmetic is decoupled from cyclotomic arithmetic rather than fused with it through a shared NTT-friendly prime basis.

The starting observation: Full RNS ties two distinct concerns together, namely the decomposition of a large coefficient into machine-word pieces (needed for arithmetic and for the digit decomposition of key switching) and the number-theoretic transform used for polynomial multiplication. Both are carried by the same family of primes, which forces every modulus to be NTT-friendly, makes rescaling granularity a function of the prime sizes, and, because basis conversion between $k$-prime bases is a quadratic operation, makes the number of NTTs in key switching scale quadratically in the number of limbs.

Belorgey, Carpov, Gama, Guasch, and Jetchev showed the two mechanisms can be fully decoupled. Building on the second gadget decomposition of Kim et al., which shifts the FHE bottleneck away from the NTT, they represent big numbers positionally, as a bivariate polynomial in which one variable carries the cyclotomic structure and the other carries a base-$2^{-K}$ digit expansion of each coefficient over the Torus $\mathbb{T} = \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$, the additive group of reals modulo 1 familiar as the plaintext and ciphertext domain of TFHE-style schemes. Any coefficient in $\mathbb{Z}_q$ embeds into $\mathbb{T}$ as the fraction $x/q$, and a base-$2^{-K}$ expansion of a Torus element is simply its fixed-point binary representation, so the digit decomposition needed for key switching is available directly from the representation, with no basis conversion at all. This makes the number of transforms in the half external product linear rather than quadratic in the number of limbs, directly targeting the dominant cost of key switching, while recovering bit-granular rescaling by simple bit shifts.

The open-source poulpy library implements this bivariate representation across a hardware abstraction layer, reporting parameterization by a single modulus bit-size rather than a hand-chosen prime chain, a common Torus plaintext space that eases scheme switching in the spirit of CHIMERA, and a flat, vectorization-friendly memory layout amenable to hardware acceleration. A CKKS evaluator (poulpy-ckks) exists as an early, experimental prototype.

The authors are careful about the status of this direction: these developments have so far been demonstrated primarily in the exact and Boolean settings (Module-LWE, TFHE/FHEW-style bootstrapping), with approximate-arithmetic support still early and experimental. Whether positional representations can serve CKKS as effectively, weighing linear-limb key switching and native precision management against highly optimized SIMD- and GPU-friendly RNS backends with mature bootstrapping implementations, is at the time of writing an open and only exploratory question. The tension is instructive: the very properties positional arithmetic recovers, arbitrary bit-granular rescaling and a scaling factor decoupled from the modulus factors, are precisely those that reduced-error scaling, composite scaling, and grafting work to reconstruct from within the residue world.

Conclusion

The evolution is best read not as progress toward a single optimal solution but as a sequence of engineering trade-offs, each generation addressing its predecessor's primary limitation while introducing new architectural constraints:

  • Arbitrary-precision arithmetic: simple and mathematically natural, poor performance.
  • CRT-based representations: dramatically faster polynomial arithmetic, but a hybrid architecture whose remaining bottleneck, the magnitude-dependent operations, resisted residue-wise treatment.
  • Full RNS: resolved that bottleneck through two primitives, fast basis extension and scaling, realized in two contrasting styles (integer-only correction-based BEHZ, floating-point estimation-based HPS). These primitives are crucial for every performance-critical procedure in modern libraries, from CKKS rescaling to hybrid key switching and bootstrapping, on CPUs and GPUs alike, at the cost of increasingly sophisticated basis management, modulus-chain design, and memory-efficient data movement.

The closing recommendation is against treating approaches as superseding one another: future implementations may benefit from revisiting alternative arithmetic backends whenever they offer a more favorable balance among performance, flexibility, and implementation complexity.

Note from the paper's acknowledgements: the authors state they used Claude for polishing and proofreading the text, reviewed the changes, and assume full responsibility for the manuscript.

Algorithms and pseudocode

Algorithm 1 is stated verbatim as it appears in the paper. The remaining listings are assembled self-contained from the paper's equations and step-by-step descriptions, which the body references without always spelling out as formal pseudocode.

Algorithm 1: Small Montgomery reduction modulo $q$ (BEHZ)

Algorithm 1  SmMRq_m~ : small Montgomery reduction modulo q   (BEHZ)

Require: c'' = [m~ * c]_q + upsilon * q, represented in B' u {m_sk, m~}
Ensure:  c' in B' u {m_sk} with c' = c'' * m~^-1 (mod q)
         and  ||c'||_inf <= ||c''||_inf / m~ + q/2

 1: r_m~  <-  [ -c''_m~ * q^-1 ]_m~
 2: for j in B' u {m_sk} do
 3:     c'_j  <-  [ (c''_j + q * r_m~) * m~^-1 ]_j
 4: end for
 5: return c'

Note: m_sk appears only as a carried residue channel; it plays no role in
      the reduction itself. The correction leaves a small additive term
      that must be tracked in the noise analysis.

Algorithm 2: BEHZ fast base conversion (approximate)

FastBaseConv(x, B, B')

Input:  x ~ (x_1, ..., x_k) in CRT form w.r.t. B = {q_1, ..., q_k}, q = prod_i q_i
        target base B' = {p_1, ..., p_k'}, coprime to B
Precomp: [ (q/q_i)^-1 ]_{q_i}  for all i
         [ q/q_i ]_{p_j}       for all i, j
Output: residues of (x + upsilon*q) w.r.t. B', for some |upsilon| <= k/2

 1: for i = 1..k do                       # channel-local, single precision
 2:     y_i <- [ x_i * [ (q/q_i)^-1 ]_{q_i} ]_{q_i}
 3: end for
 4: for each p_j in B' do
 5:     out_j <- [ sum_{i=1..k} y_i * [ q/q_i ]_{p_j} ]_{p_j}
 6: end for
 7: return (out_j)_{p_j in B'}

The quotient upsilon of the reconstruction identity is never computed, so the
result is congruent to x modulo q only up to the q-overflow upsilon*q.
Either tolerate it (it inflates noise), or remove it:
  - input side : pre-multiply by m~, then SmMRq_m~ (Algorithm 1)
  - output side: Shenoy-Kumaresan exact return via the carried modulus m_sk

Algorithm 3: HPS fast basis extension (exact)

FastBaseExt(x, B, B')

Input:  x ~ (x_1, ..., x_k) w.r.t. B = {q_1, ..., q_k}, q = prod_i q_i
        target base B' = {p_1, ..., p_k'}, coprime to B
Precomp: [ (q/q_i)^-1 ]_{q_i},  [ q/q_i ]_{p_j},  [ q ]_{p_j}
Output: exact residues of x w.r.t. B'   (no auxiliary moduli needed)

 1: for i = 1..k do                       # integer, single precision
 2:     y_i <- [ x_i * [ (q/q_i)^-1 ]_{q_i} ]_{q_i}
 3: end for
 4: # the only non-integer step: estimate the reconstruction quotient
 5: upsilon <- round( sum_{i=1..k} ( y_i / q_i ) )      # floating point
 6: for each p_j in B' do
 7:     out_j <- [ sum_{i=1..k} y_i * [ q/q_i ]_{p_j}  -  upsilon * [ q ]_{p_j} ]_{p_j}
 8: end for
 9: return (out_j)_{p_j in B'}

Precision: each summand y_i/q_i lies in [-1/2, 1/2), so with IEEE 754 doubles
the per-term error is < 2^-53 and the total error eps satisfies |eps| < k*2^-53.
An off-by-one occurs only if the exact sum lands in Z + 1/2 +- eps:
  - provably never when |x| << q (e.g. |x| < q/4),
  - probability <= 2|eps| for (pseudo)random x in Z_q,
  - and even then it adds q, i.e. at most 1-2 bits of ciphertext noise.
No constraint on the moduli sizes: full word-sized q_i work with plain doubles.

Algorithm 4: HPS simple scaling (BFV decryption pattern)

SimpleScale_HPS(x, B, t)

Input:  x ~ (x_1, ..., x_k) w.r.t. B, q = prod_i q_i;  integer t >= 2, t << q
Output: y = [ round( (t/q) * x ) ]_t
Precomp: split the rational constants into integer and fractional parts
         ( t * [ (q/q_i)^-1 ]_{q_i} ) / q_i  =  omega_i + theta_i
         omega_i in Z_t          stored as single-precision integers
         theta_i in [-1/2, 1/2)  stored as (extended) doubles

 1: w <- [ sum_{i=1..k} x_i * omega_i ]_t          # integer arithmetic
 2: v <- round( sum_{i=1..k} x_i * theta_i )       # floating point
 3: return [ w + v ]_t

Exactness for decryption: ciphertext noise keeps the pre-rounding value within
1/4 of an integer, so it suffices that  q_i <= 2^(nu-1) / k,  where nu is the
significand precision in bits. This tightens the textbook correctness bound by
at most one bit, from (Delta - r_t(q))/2 to (Delta - r_t(q))/4, with
Delta = floor(q/t) and r_t(q) = q - t*Delta.

Unlike basis extension, HERE the float precision constrains the moduli size,
because theta_i (absolute error ~2^-nu) multiplies a full-sized residue x_i:
    nu = 53  (double)         : restricted moduli
    nu = 65  (x86 long double): up to 59-bit moduli
    nu = 113 (software double-double): full 60-bit range, large slowdown
Kim-Polyakov-Zucca removed this constraint by decomposing the input residues
into smaller digits before the floating-point summation, supporting the full
60-bit range with plain double precision.

Algorithm 5: BEHZ simple scaling (integer-only)

SimpleScale_BEHZ(x, B, t, gamma)

Input:  x ~ (x_1, ..., x_k) w.r.t. B, q = prod_i q_i;  t >= 2;
        redundant modulus gamma
Output: y ~ [ round( (t/q) * x ) ]_t

Identity used (exact integer division, flooring instead of rounding):
        floor( (t/q) * [x]_q )  =  ( t*[x]_q  -  |t*x|_q ) / q

 1: # modulo t the first term cancels, so only -|t*x|_q / q is needed
 2: carry out the computation simultaneously in the bases {t} and {gamma}
 3: obtain -|t*x|_q / q via FastBaseConv from base q to {t, gamma}
 4: use the gamma-channel to (a) cancel the q-overflow of the inexact
    conversion and (b) correct the flooring-vs-rounding discrepancy
 5: return the corrected t-channel result

Correctness requires  ||e||_inf <= Delta*(1/2 - k/gamma) - |q|_t / 2,
which approaches the textbook bound only as gamma >> k.

Algorithm 6: HPS complex scaling (scale out of an extended base)

ComplexScale_HPS(x, B u B', t)

Input:  x in Z n [ -qp/(2t), qp/(2t) ), represented in
        B u B' = {q_1..q_k, p_1..p_k'};  q = prod_i q_i, p = prod_j p_j, Q = q*p
Output: y = [ round( (t/q) * x ) ]_q,  i.e. scaled and back in base B
Precomp: ( t * [ (Q/q_i)^-1 ]_{q_i} * p ) / q_i  =  omega'_i + theta'_i
             omega'_i in Z_p,  theta'_i in [-1/2, 1/2)
         lambda_j := [ t * [ (Q/p_j)^-1 ]_{p_j} * (p/p_j) ]_{p_j}

 Step 1 -- scale within the complementary base B'
   (this is SimpleScale with q' = q*p and t' = t*p)
 1: v <- round( sum_{i=1..k} theta'_i * x_i )          # computed once
 2: for each p_j in B' do
 3:     y'_j <- [ lambda_j * x'_j + sum_{i=1..k} [omega'_i]_{p_j} * x_i + v ]_{p_j}
 4: end for
    # since |x| < qp/(2t), the scaled value lies in [-p/2, p/2), so the
    # mod-p representation determines y' exactly, with no modular reduction

 Step 2 -- extend back
 5: y <- FastBaseExt(y', B', B)          # Algorithm 3
 6: discard the B' components
 7: return y

Because |y'| <= q/2 << p/2, this second extension provably never lands in the
floating-point error region: exactness is free from the choice p > q. Rounding
here need not be exact; a rounding error only adds to the ciphertext noise
(unlike decryption, where exactness is required).

BEHZ counterpart: same blueprint with integer-only tools -- lift via
FastBaseConv with input-side pre-multiplication by m~ and SmMRq_m~
(Algorithm 1) to remove q-overflows, approximate flooring in the complementary
base, and an exact return via Shenoy-Kumaresan using the carried modulus m_sk.
The channels {m~, m_sk} ride along through the tensor product, adding NTTs and
modular multiplications throughout.

Algorithm 7: Modulus switching / CKKS rescaling in RNS

ModSwitch(c, level l)          # in CKKS this is Rescale

Input:  c in R_{Q_l}, with Q_l = prod_{i=0..l} q_i
Output: c' in R_{Q_{l-1}},  Q_{l-1} = Q_l / q_l,  c' = round( c / q_l )
Precomp: [ q_l^-1 ]_{q_i}  for i < l

 1: obtain [c]_{q_l}                 # one iNTT in the dropped channel if c is
                                     # kept in evaluation representation
 2: broadcast [c]_{q_l} into the remaining channels
 3: for i = 0 .. l-1 do
 4:     c'_i <- [ q_l^-1 * ( c_i - [c]_{q_l} ) ]_{q_i}
 5: end for
 6: return c'

Cost: one iNTT plus one modular multiplication per remaining channel. No
generic scaling procedure is needed because q_l is itself an RNS modulus.
BGV adds a correction to preserve the plaintext value.

Consequences and the three fixes:
  - granularity is tied to the chain: you can only divide by primes (or
    products of primes) actually present in it
  - q_l ~ 2^Delta but never exactly, so every rescaling perturbs the scale
    (the RNS scaling error, absent from multiprecision CKKS)
  - reduced-error CKKS : track an exact level-dependent scale,
    Delta_{l-1} = Delta_l^2 / q_l, inserting scalar corrections when
    operands at different scales meet  (OpenFHE FLEXIBLEAUTO/-EXT)
  - composite scaling  : build each scale from d >= 2 primes with
    prod_{j=1..d} q_{l,j} ~ 2^Delta, dropping d primes at once
  - grafting           : assemble the modulus from reusable word-size
    "sprouts" (including non-NTT power-of-two factors) and rescale by an
    arbitrary bit count as a modulus-switching step

Algorithm 8: Hybrid key switching in RNS

HybridKeySwitch(c, {ksk_j}, d)

Input:  c in R_{Q_l} in evaluation (NTT) form, decryptable under s'
        base B_{Q_l} = {q_1, ..., q_k} partitioned into d digit groups
        D_1, ..., D_d with partial products Qhat_j = prod_{q_i in D_j} q_i
        special base B_P = {p_1, ..., p_k'} with P = prod_j p_j and
        P >~ max_j Qhat_j        # one digit's worth, NOT all of Q_l
        keys ksk_j in R^2_{Q_l P} encrypting
          [ P * [ (Q_l/Qhat_j)^-1 ]_{Qhat_j} * (Q_l/Qhat_j) * s' ]_{Q_l P}
Output: ciphertext in R^2_{Q_l} decryptable under s

 1: # step 1 -- decompose (free residue split)
 2: iNTT c into coefficient representation                    # k iNTTs
 3: for j = 1..d do
 4:     c^(j) <- ( [c]_{q_i} )_{q_i in D_j}      # |c^(j)| <= Qhat_j / 2
 5: end for
 6: # step 2 -- ModUp: the one step needing cross-channel magnitude info
 7: for j = 1..d do
 8:     cU^(j) <- FastBaseExt( c^(j), D_j, B_{Q_l} u B_P )    # or FastBaseConv
 9:     NTT cU^(j) into evaluation representation             # d(k+k') NTTs
10: end for
11: # step 3 -- inner product, entirely component-wise
12: acc <- sum_{j=1..d}  cU^(j) (*) ksk_j
13: # step 4 -- ModDown: complex scaling by 1/P (Algorithm 6, bases swapped)
14: out <- [ round( acc / P ) ]_{Q_l}
15: NTT out back to evaluation representation
16: return out

The digit-count knob d:
    d = k       one prime per digit: minimal P, hence the most modulus
                budget for depth; most NTTs; largest key material
    1 < d < k   practical choice, balancing key size, noise budget and the
                O( d*(k + k') ) NTT cost that dominates runtime
    d = 1       GHS: single digit; P > Q_l halves the usable modulus
                budget; fewest NTTs

ModDown needs no concluding extension: the result is wanted only in B_{Q_l},
which is the complementary base here, so step 1 of complex scaling already
produces it. The factor P attenuates the key noise, and the ModDown rounding
error only adds to the noise.

Algorithm 9: BFV homomorphic multiplication as a composition

BFV.Mult(ct1, ct2)

 1: lift both ciphertexts from B_q to B_q u B_p        # basis extension,
                                                       # 4 conversions total
                                                       # qp >~ largest tensored
                                                       # coefficient
 2: compute the tensor product in the extended base    # component-wise
 3: scale the three resulting components by t/q back into B_q
                                                       # complex scaling,
                                                       # 3 invocations
 4: relinearize the quadratic component via RNS-digit key switching
 5: return the relinearized ciphertext

BFV.Decrypt: a single simple-scaling invocation (Algorithm 4 or 5).

The cost of the whole pipeline is exactly the sum of these building-block
costs, which is why the BEHZ/HPS comparison transfers unchanged to any scheme
assembled from the same blocks.
